articles.title: FHIR in Focus: Enabling Biomedical Data Harmonization for Intelligent Healthcare Systems
articles.content: Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), developed by Health Level Seven International (HL7), has emerged as the leading healthcare data standard to address persistent barriers in interoperability, fragmented exchange, and inconsistent data harmonization. As health systems worldwide undergo digital transformation, FHIR offers a flexible framework for integrating electronic health records, analytics platforms, and decision-support tools. Its growth has been accelerated by policy mandates such as the 21st Century Cures Act, as well as the availability of application programming interfaces (APIs), software development kits (SDKs), and web standards. Globally, FHIR has been adopted or piloted by national health systems in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia, and incorporated into World Health Organization data initiatives, underscoring its role in global digital health strategy. Documented outcomes of this review include comprehensive mapping of FHIR applications across clinical, research, and public health domains; identification of adoption barriers and enablers; insights into integration with generative AI and large language models for predictive modeling, automated documentation, and decision support; and guidance for future innovations such as blockchain-enabled infrastructure and cloud-native scalability. Nonetheless, challenges remain, including uneven implementation, workforce training gaps, scalability limitations, and unresolved concerns around privacy, security, and regulatory compliance. This synthesis provides actionable insights for providers, researchers, policymakers, and developers to advance global health interoperability.

articles.title: Network Models of Neurodegeneration: Bridging Neuronal Dynamics and Disease Progression
articles.content: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by the accumulation of misfolded proteins and widespread disruptions in brain function. Computational modeling has advanced our understanding of these processes, but efforts have traditionally focused on either neuronal dynamics or the biological processes underlying disease. One class of models uses neural mass and whole-brain frameworks to simulate changes in oscillations, connectivity, and network stability. A second class focuses on biological processes underlying disease progression, particularly prion-like propagation through the connectome, glial responses and vascular mechanisms. Each modeling tradition has provided important insights, but experimental evidence shows these processes are interconnected: neuronal activity modulates protein release and clearance, while pathological burden disrupts neuronal function. Modeling these domains in isolation limits our understanding, although recent studies have begun to bridge the two by coupling neuronal and pathological processes. To determine where and why disease emerges, how it spreads, and how it might be altered, mathematical models that capture feedback between neuronal dynamics and disease biology are needed. This review surveys the two modeling approaches and highlights efforts to unify them, emphasizing that linking neuronal activity and disease progression is key to identifying strategies that slow, halt, or reverse degeneration and restore neural function.

articles.title: Emerging Noninvasive Approaches for the Suppression of Pathological Tremor
articles.content: Pathological tremor affects over 40 million people worldwide, significantly impairing daily activities and quality of life. Pharmacological treatments show limited efficacy, with up to 30% discontinuation rates, while surgical interventions like deep brain stimulation achieve significant tremor reduction but are often unsuitable due to age, comorbidities, or personal preference. Recently, the need for safe and effective alternatives has led to the development of innovative, noninvasive, and patient-friendly technologies for tremor management. This clinical application review analyzed 134 studies (1969-2025), categorizing them into three major modalities, focusing on their underlying neurophysiological mechanisms, with a special emphasis on the clinical perspective. The three considered modalities were force-controlling (orthoses and functional electrical stimulation), central neuromodulation (transcranial magnetic stimulation, transcranial electrical stimulation, low-intensity focused ultrasound, and transcutaneous spinal cord stimulation), and peripheral neuromodulation (afferent stimulation and vibration). Force-controlling strategies showed promising acute effects, though clinical translation remains limited by poor wearability and the development of muscle fatigue. Central neuromodulation produced moderate effects, while peripheral neuromodulation has gained clinical traction, with several devices now being commercially available. However, heterogeneity in study design, patient populations, and technology maturity remain the main obstacles for the direct comparison of techniques. Future research should prioritize larger multicenter trials, standardized outcome measures, and accessibility considerations to enable personalized, evidence-based treatment selection for diverse tremor populations.

articles.title: Assistive Trajectory Planning for Lower Limb Exoskeletons: Strategies From Laboratory-Optimized Gait to Environmentally-Adaptive Locomotion Through Multimodal Parameter Awareness
articles.content: Lower limb assistive exoskeletons (LLEs) show great potential to reduce metabolic cost, improve walking performance, and correct abnormal gait patterns. Among their core control architectures, assistive trajectory planning is key to determining system responsiveness and effectiveness under varying locomotion conditions. Many trajectory planning methods were proposed in either laboratory or unstructured real-world environments. To clarify the scope and challenges of existing research, this review categorizes trajectory planning strategies into two major types based on application scenarios: (1) strategies for laboratory settings with controllable disturbances, which usually involve optimal control for gait under stable or controllable conditions; and (2) strategies for real-world environments characterized by varying terrain, individual differences, and gait fluctuations, which usually involve adaptive control for gait under diverse or unstructured conditions. Given the foundational role of gait phase detection in trajectory planning, this review also systematically examines mainstream algorithms for gait phase recognition and estimation. Finally, the paper analyzes the limitations of existing methods and discusses the potential of advanced algorithms, intelligent multimodal sensing systems, novel sensing technologies, and embedded deployment to enhance the performance of exoskeleton assistive trajectory planning.

articles.title: Gentle touch modulates late spinal and cortical somatosensory responses without detectable changes in spinal component N13 and nociceptive flexion reflex amplitude
articles.content:
Affective and gentle touch have been associated with changes in pain and somatosensory perception, but it remains unclear whether these effects reflect early spinal gating or later cortical and descending processes.

We investigated whether gentle touch with CT-optimal characteristics modulates spinal and cortical somatosensory and nociceptive processing across three experiments. Experiment 1 compared the sural-nerve nociceptive flexion reflex (NFR; RIII) in the leg while the forearm received no touch, vibration, robot-delivered brushing, or human-delivered stroking. Experiment 2 compared somatosensory evoked potentials (SEPs) across the same four conditions. Experiment 3 compared robot-delivered brushing with no touch, including additional trials to improve sensitivity to spinal SEP modulations.

RIII amplitudes and spinal (N13, P22) and cortical (N20, P25, N30, P45, N60, P150) SEP components were analyzed. Gentle touch modulated neither the heterosegmental NFR nor the segmental N13, arguing against inhibition of early afferent transmission within or beyond the touched segment. However, Experiment 3 revealed modulation of the P22 spinal component, suggesting that gentle touch may influence spinal processing through supraspinal feedback mechanisms. At the cortical level, both robot- and human-delivered gentle touch attenuated the N60 and P150 components relative to vibration and no-touch conditions, indicating modulation of later stages of somatosensory processing consistent with attentional and cognitive influences.

These findings suggest that CT-optimal gentle touch does not act through direct segmental inhibition of incoming sensory signals, but instead modulates later spinal and cortical processing, likely through descending influences.

This study provides a multilevel neurophysiological framework for understanding how affective touch shapes sensory processing.
articles.author: Ribeiro-Carreira, A., Carvalho, L., Oliveira, M., da-Silva, M., Eippert, F., Coutinho, J., Olausson, H., Sampaio, A., Gonzalez-Villar, A. J.

articles.title: Longitudinal Increases in Ventral Attention Network Connectivity Predict Heightened Reward and Punishment Sensitivities via Self-Control Decline in Emerging Adulthood
articles.content: Emerging adulthood is a critical developmental window for the maturation of executive control and the reorganization of intrinsic brain networks. However, the longitudinal neurobiological mechanisms underlying changes in cognitive control?and their associations with trait sensitivities?remain poorly understood. In a two-year longitudinal study, 332 emerging adults underwent behavioral assessments and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Latent Change Score Modeling (LCSM) revealed that longitudinal increases in reward and punishment sensitivities were primarily predicted by the progressive decline in self-control, rather than baseline or concurrent impulsivity. Neurally, by targeting the macroscopic connectome utilizing rigorous change score models adjusted for baseline variances and longitudinal head motion, we found that longitudinal increases in intra-network connectivity within the Ventral Attention Network (VAN) specifically and robustly tracked this self-control decline. Furthermore, a unified path analysis revealed a robust full mediation mechanism: heightened VAN intra-network connectivity predicted increased environmental sensitivities strictly through the decline in self-control. These findings identify increased VAN connectivity as a specific neural marker of diminished cognitive control, highlighting the preservation of self-control capacity as a key mechanistic target for promoting adaptive resilience during emerging adulthood.
articles.author: He, J., Zhao, H., Lei, X., Qiu, J., Feng, T., Chen, H., Turel, O., He, Q.

articles.title: Developmental timing of gene expression predicts dosage dominance, which tracks neuronal-glial fate in the developing human brain
articles.content: Genes implicated in brain disorders have diverse functions, but how altered dosage shapes their effects on developmental cell fate remains unclear. In a cell-state dynamics model of the developing human brain, genes expressed earlier in development responded more strongly to knockout than to overexpression, and this dosage dominance tracked neuronal-glial fate. Fate responses of 14,044 genes formed 31 modules across 21 lineages. Stronger perturbations could reverse fate responses despite correlated predicted expression changes across neuronal destinations. Disease-risk genes occupied shared and distinct developmental programs. Within autism, module timing distinguished genes associated with and without intellectual disability or developmental delay, while de novo and common variation implicated different modules. Knockout signatures of selected autism-associated modules matched the neuronal-down, glial-up pattern that postmortem autism cortex shares with other psychiatric disorders. These findings connect heterogeneous genetic risk through developmental programs whose fate responses depend on dosage and cellular context.
articles.author: Koh, I. G., Shin, D.-M., Kim, B., Chung, S., Kim, S.-W., Lee, H., Son, J. H., Lee, J., Bong, G., Han, J., Chung, C., Yoo, H. J., An, J.-Y.

articles.title: Altered ultrasonic vocalizations in mouse models of FOXG1 syndrome
articles.content: FOXG1 syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder with communication impairment as a defining clinical feature, yet vocal behavior has not been characterized in animal models of FOXG1. We examined neonatal ultrasonic vocalizations in two mouse models that disrupt Foxg1 in distinct developmental and cellular contexts: a NEX-Cre-driven conditional heterozygous model targeting postmitotic cortical and hippocampal excitatory neurons, and a W300X/+ knock-in model carrying a patient derived truncating mutation at the endogenous Foxg1 locus. Vocalizations were recorded at postnatal day 7 and analyzed for call number, duration, frequency range, and repertoire composition. The two models exhibited distinct vocal phenotypes. Conditional heterozygous mice produced longer calls while total vocal output, frequency range, and repertoire composition were preserved. In contrast, W300X/+ mice produced shorter calls, showed a significant shift in repertoire composition, and a non-significant trend toward reduced vocal output. The effect of genotype on call duration differed significantly between models, demonstrating opposing effects on temporal vocal structure. Frequency range was not significantly altered by genotype in either model, although sex was associated with frequency range in the conditional heterozygous cohort. These findings provide the first evidence that Foxg1 disruption alters neonatal vocal behavior and show that the resulting phenotype depends on the developmental, cellular, and molecular context of the mutation. Neonatal vocalizations therefore provide a sensitive behavioral readout for distinguishing functional consequences of disease relevant FOXG1 perturbations.
articles.author: Abdavinejad, S., Shin, D., Kwak, E., Hwang, H., Jeon, S., Maltbie, P., Lee, S.-K., Dent, M. L., Duvvuru, V.

articles.title: Automated neuroimaging meta-analysis through LLM-guided selection improves recovery of published spatial patterns
articles.content: Systematic meta-analysis enables cumulative science, but expert-led, manual workflows do not scale with the growing literature. In neuroimaging, automated frameworks are widely used but typically sacrifice precision by using coarse article selection and pooling reported results, combining different tasks, populations or comparisons even when only a subset is relevant. Here we present AutoNIMA, a large language model (LLM)-guided framework that screens articles using expert-defined eligibility criteria and parses heterogeneous tables to extract brain stereotactic coordinates and select relevant analyses within each article. AutoNIMA produced maps more closely matching expert-curated references than a search-only baseline representing existing automated methods in 26 of 27 meta-analyses. Analysis-level selection accounted for most of the improvement. These findings demonstrate how LLM-guided curation can filter relevant analyses within the same paper and support scalable neuroimaging evidence synthesis.
articles.author: de la Vega, A., Kent, J. D., Yang, A., Nichols, T. E., Poline, J.-B., Bottenhorn, K. L., Chen, Z., Poldrack, R. A., Laird, A. R.

articles.title: Loss of TTC5 impairs cortical development, disrupts tubulin homeostasis and progenitor mitosis in vivo
articles.content: Objective Loss-of-function mutations in the multifunctional scaffolding protein tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) cause Neurodevelopmental Disorder with Cerebral Atrophy and variable Facial Dysmorphism (NEDCAFD), a recently described neurogenetic syndrome. TTC5 autoregulates tubulin translation in vitro; however, the role of TTC5 in brain development in vivo is poorly understood. Here, we define the function of TTC5 in neocortical development. Methods We established a mouse model carrying a recurrent patient nonsense mutation (TTC5R263*/R263*) causing NEDCAFD, and investigated cortical progenitor development, tubulin homeostasis, microtubule function, and neuronal morphogenesis using in vivo, in vitro, and transcriptomic approaches. Results The TTC5R263* mutation was a strong loss-of-function allele, with homozygous newborns exhibiting neonatal lethality, reduced brain size, and loss of cortical neurons. These developmental abnormalities arise from an early and persistent loss of neural progenitor expansion and impaired neuronal differentiation during corticogenesis, associated with defective mitotic progression, altered cell fate determination, and increased DNA damage. We further investigate TTC5 as a regulator of tubulin homeostasis during cortical development in vivo. Loss of TTC5 reduced tubulin mRNA and protein levels. Furthermore, TTC5R263*/R263* primary neurons exhibit reduced microtubule growth dynamics and defective neuronal arborization. Transcriptomic analyses of TTC5R263*/R263* developing cortex identify differentially expressed genes and pathways involved in neurodevelopmental processes, including coordinated dysregulation of cell-cycle regulators and a multitude of microtubule-associated gene pathways. Interpretation TTC5 is essential for cortical progenitor expansion, mitotic progression, and tubulin homeostasis during cortical development. These findings establish a mechanistic framework for NEDCAFD pathogenesis in vivo.
articles.author: Li, Z., Ma, L., Riaz, H. A., Wu, Q., Schmidt, M., Fleishman, M., Morrow, E. M.

articles.title: Auditory cortical population codes for pitch are cue dependent
articles.content: Pitch provides a powerful example of perceptual invariance, enabling us to recognize the same melody across different instruments. The fundamental frequency (F0) at which a pitch is heard can be derived from either the harmonic spacing of frequency components (spectral cues), the waveform periodicity (temporal cues), or both. It is unclear whether population codes for F0 in auditory cortex are invariant across these acoustic cue classes. We addressed this question by training a linear decoder to predict F0 from the spiking responses of 1085 neurons in ferret primary auditory cortex to 10 sound types varying in their spectral and temporal composition. F0 could be decoded accurately when trained and tested on any individual sound type. However, decoding performance generalised well across sounds only if they contained the same class of pitch cue, and poorly between complex sounds and pure tones. Onset and offset responses carried different information about the F0 of complex sounds. Finally, approximately 20 neurons were sufficient to decode F0, but F0 information was widely distributed across the neural population. These findings show that F0 is represented in primary auditory cortex in cue-dependent, temporally multiplexed subspaces, with sparse pitch representations embedded in a distributed, robust population code.
articles.author: Tarka, V. M., Gaucher, Q., King, A. J., Willmore, B. D., Walker, K. M. M.

articles.title: β-Adrenergic regulation of mGluR5-dependent Ca2+ signalling in reactive astrocytes
articles.content: Astrocytes support neuronal function and brain homeostasis and undergo structural and functional remodelling under pathological conditions. Here, we compared astrocytes maintained in serum-containing medium, modelling a blood-brain barrier-compromised reactive state, with serum-free conditions that promote a more physiological arborised phenotype. We examined surface expression and signalling of metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5), {beta}-adrenergic receptors ({beta}-ARs), and pituitary adenylate cyclase-activating polypeptide type 1 receptor (PAC1) as well as expression of excitatory amino acid transporter 2 (EAAT2). Live-cell immunolabelling combined with optophysiological measurements revealed that serum-exposed reactive astrocytes had substantially reduced surface mGluR5 expression and negligible mGluR5-dependent Ca2+ signalling, accompanied by increased expression of EAAT2. Adrenergic stimulation and sustained cAMP elevation restored surface mGluR5 expression and (S)-3,5-dihydroxyphenylglycine (DHPG)-evoked Ca2+ responses while reducing EAAT2 expression despite continued serum exposure. Reactive astrocytes also showed enhanced, prolonged {beta}-AR-mediated cAMP responses that were largely uncoupled from changes in intracellular Ca2+. These findings demonstrate coordinated remodelling of glutamatergic and {beta}-adrenergic signalling in reactive astrocytes. The capacity to restore mGluR5-dependent signalling is retained and strongly regulated by cAMP, suggesting that neuromodulatory pathways can modulate astrocytic glutamate responsiveness independently of a complete reversal of the reactive phenotype.
articles.author: Stenovec, M., Pirnat, S., Vrsnik, J., Dolinar, K., Verkhratsky, A., Zorec, R.

articles.title: The Developing Human Connectome Project: Fetal Data Release
articles.content: The Developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP) represents a large open science resource designed to enable detailed investigations of typical and atypical brain development across the perinatal period. It consists of 1228 multimodal magnetic resonance image examinations of the fetal and/or neonatal brain from 1173 participants, together with collateral demographic, clinical, family, neurocognitive and genomic data. All subjects were studied in utero and/or soon after birth with a single MRI scanner using specially developed scanning sequences with novel motion-tolerant imaging methods and optimised for the changing properties of the developing brain. The neonatal data has been described and released separately. The fetal data release consists of multimodal data from 273 subjects scanned between 20 + 6 and 38+2 weeks (+days) of gestation, with some fetuses imaged more than once to provide longitudinal data creating 297 datasets in total. The data include: high resolution and motion corrected T1 and T2 weighted anatomical images; high temporal resolution functional and multi-shell high angular resolution diffusion MRI; and multimodal age-resolved atlases; together with demographic, family and clinical data, genomic and epigenomic data and follow-up neurodevelopmental assessment at around 18 months. This paper describes the dHCP fetal image acquisition, reconstruction and processing protocols, summarizes the available data, and provides information on how it can be accessed.

articles.title: The metacognitive signatures of imposterism
articles.content: The imposter phenomenon (or imposterism) is a commonly reported psychological pattern in which individuals persistently doubt their abilities and accomplishments despite objective evidence of their competence. Imposterism is associated with chronic self-doubt and reduced well-being, yet its cognitive mechanisms remain unclear. In a large online sample (N = 602), we investigated how self-reported imposter feelings relate to decision-making, confidence and information search in a perceptual decision-making task. Imposterism was associated with lower confidence in perceptual decisions and increased information seeking, despite not being associated with any detriment in objective perceptual performance. Though symptoms of anxiety and depression contributed to the relationship between imposterism and confidence, imposterism uniquely predicted increased information-seeking. Interestingly, the increased information seeking associated with imposterism did not lead to an imposterism-specific increase in final decision performance and did not alleviate overall uncertainty: imposterism remained associated with reduced confidence even for final decisions. To explain this, we hypothesised that information seeking may compensate for maladaptive second-guessing. Supporting this, imposterism predicted greater response switching and decreases in accuracy on trials where no additional information was sought, reflecting counterproductive changes of mind. These effects were absent on trials where information was accessed, suggesting that seeking additional information helped buffer against maladaptive second-guessing. Overall, our findings show that imposterism is marked by low confidence, heightened information seeking, and vulnerability to second-guessing in the absence of external reassurance. These results provide novel insights into distortions of self-evaluation in imposterism and highlight a compensatory role for information seeking in stabilising performance. Our study advances understanding of a widely discussed yet underexplored psychological phenomenon with significant implications for education, workplace wellbeing, and mental health.
